text: Caldwell Ridge Analytics' four-lesson network project pulled on every chapter of this course, not just the module chapter. This lesson traces each decision back to the chapter that actually made it possible, then closes the course and points to what's next.

Chapter 1 is why required_providers and a plain init/plan/apply loop needed no introduction in Lesson 29. Chapter 2 is why real azurerm resource types felt ordinary rather than new. Chapter 3 is the backbone of the remote backend, state locking, and Lesson 31's entire recovery process -- state pull, state list, state rm, and import are Chapter 3's toolkit, used on a real incident.

Chapter 4 is the reason there was only ever one modules/network source, with variables for address space and subnet count instead of hard-coded values. Chapter 5 is exactly what made Lesson 30 possible: .tfvars per environment, and the reasoned choice of directory-per-environment state over a shared workspace. Chapter 7's plan-on-pull-request, approval gate, and drift detection are what should catch a Lesson 31-style incident before it ever reaches a confusing Monday-morning error.

Across four lessons, Caldwell Ridge built one reusable module, deployed it twice at two different sizes from two isolated state files, and recovered a production resource from a manual, out-of-band deletion by backing up state first and choosing deliberately between state rm and import. That's the real job: writing HCL that survives being reused, re-run, and occasionally repaired.

Chapter 6's Bicep deep dive doesn't appear directly in this Azure project, but it's why the provider choice itself was a real decision -- Terraform and Bicep solve overlapping problems with different tradeoffs, and knowing both is what let this capstone pick Terraform on purpose. This course is now complete; the Advanced Specialization stage keeps going from here.

Terraform, Bicep & Infrastructure as Code is done: fundamentals, provisioning, state, modules, environments, Bicep, and CI/CD, proven on one real project across dev and prod, including a real incident recovered start to finish. Next up in this path: Docker, Kubernetes & Container Platforms.
